To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is limited evidence on the use of PROMs in children and young people with allergy and asthma in the clinical setting.
there is increasing recognition of patient‐reported outcome measures as at least as valuable as traditional objective measures of health.

there is increasing recognition of importance of patient's perspectives and their assessments of healthcare processes, but there is limited evidence on using PROMs for children with allergy or asthma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new PROMs for allergic diseases in children and their use in routine clinical care.
the development and evaluation of PROMs for use in allergy and asthma in young children and adolescents.
the development, testing and evaluation of PROMs for allergy in children.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a paucity of evidence on the use of PROMs in routine clinical care for children with allergy and asthma.
we need more evidence on how PROMs for allergy in children can be used in clinical practice and research.
the use of patient‐reported outcome measures is an area of unexplored potential in allergy and asthma in the pediatric population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are a limited number of PROMs available for allergy and asthma, but there is little evidence on how they can be incorporated in clinical practice.
there is a need for more PROMs for allergy, and in particular asthma, for children and that there are few data on the acceptability and feasibility of these instruments.

there are some validated PROMs for allergy, but there are few that have been used in routine clinical settings and even fewer that have been used to evaluate the impact of interventions on health‐related quality of life.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a paucity of PROMs available for children with allergy and asthma.
there is a need for further research into the use of PROMs in routine clinical care for allergic diseases in children.
there is a pressing need to develop, evaluate, and implement a core set of pediatric PROMs to be used in routine clinical care for the major allergic conditions.
